nameStory: The Trailrunner lichen gets its sporty name from its habit of growing along forest paths and trails where hikers and runners pass by daily. Unlike many lichens that prefer undisturbed spots, this hardy species seems to thrive in the slightly disturbed conditions found along well-used woodland trails.
description: Trailrunner is a medium-sized foliose lichen that forms leafy, overlapping patches on tree bark and occasionally rocks. It typically grows 2-4 inches across with distinctive narrow, ribbon-like lobes that give it an almost fringed appearance. The lichen has a grayish-green color when dry that becomes more vibrant green when wet, and its edges often curl upward slightly, creating interesting shadows and textures.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The upper surface feels smooth to slightly rough, like fine sandpaper, with tiny hair-like projections (cilia) visible along the lobe edges that give it a delicate fringed look

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms leafy, overlapping patches with narrow lobes that are typically 2-5mm wide and often curl upward at the tips

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale grayish-green to brownish-gray when dry, becoming brighter green when moist; underside is typically black with a narrow brown margin

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Most commonly found on the bark of deciduous trees, especially maples and oaks, occasionally on smooth rocks

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches range from 1-4 inches across, with lobes extending outward from a central attachment point

habitat: Trailrunner favors the bark of hardwood trees in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly at low to moderate elevations. It's commonly spotted along hiking trails and forest edges where there's partial shade and good air circulation. You'll often find it growing alongside other common bark lichens on maples, oaks, and birches.

seasonality.spring: Fresh spring rains bring out the vibrant green coloration, making identification easier as the lichen becomes more pliable and the fringed edges are more apparent.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen appears more grayish and brittle, with edges often curled upward. Look for it in shadier spots where it retains some moisture.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for observation as falling leaves expose more trunk surface and autumn moisture keeps the lichen colorful and flexible.
seasonality.winter: Still visible but often appears darker and more contracted. Snow and ice can make the fringed edges particularly striking when backlit.

funFact: Despite being called 'Trailrunner,' this lichen actually grows incredibly slowly - a patch the size of a quarter may be decades old, meaning some specimens along your favorite hiking trail could have been there since before you were born!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other wrinkle lichens in the same genus, but Trailrunner's distinctive hair-like fringe along the lobe edges sets it apart. Remember: if it looks fringed and feels slightly fuzzy at the edges, it's likely your Trailrunner.
contextualKnowledge: [UNCERTAIN CLAIM] The scientific name 'ciliaris' refers to the hair-like projections (cilia) along the edges, though the exact etymology and some ecological details of this relatively uncommon species may need verification as observation data in New England is limited.
compareHints: Trailrunner differs from its cousin Fringed Wrinkle Lichen by having more pronounced cilia and typically narrower lobes. Compared to variable wrinkle-lichen, Trailrunner maintains more consistent coloring and has more regular lobe patterns. The Chestnut Wrinkle Lichen tends to be browner overall and lacks the distinctive fringing that makes Trailrunner special.

relatedSpecies.distinction: **[Uncertain claim flag]** Compared to Variable Wrinkle-lichen, Fringed Wrinkle Lichen has much more prominent and consistently present fringe hairs along its edges.

Variable wrinkle-lichen differs from its relatives by having the most pronounced wrinkled texture - fringed wrinkle-lichen has hair-like projections along edges, while trailrunner forms more elongated, strap-like lobes.
